title: The sign that turns, and the rule taken out on the road
summary: Finish inequalities with compound ranges, number line pictures and the flip derived on the line rather than decreed, then take the odd corner rule out on real streets and set a one stroke puzzle of your own.
materials: jumbo sidewalk chalk and a driveway
field journal, pencil and a ruler
graph paper for the number lines
a printed street map of your own block, or a drawn one

problems.prompt: About how many grains of sand would fill a coffee mug?
explanation: A grain of sand is about half a millimetre across, so about 20 grains fit along a centimetre.
One cubic centimetre then holds 20 by 20 by 20 grains, which is 8,000.
A mug is a few hundred cubic centimetres, and a few hundred lots of 8,000 reaches the millions.
problems.useAgain: when the thing you are counting is far too small and too many to count, and one small lump of it can be sized instead.
hints: Start with one grain. About how many would fit along a centimetre?
Fill one cubic centimetre first, before you try to fill the whole mug.
problems.socraticHint: Nobody counts sand. What is the smallest lump of it you could honestly count, and how many of those lumps fit in a mug?

variant.prompt: About how many grains of rice would fill the same mug?

problems.prompt: About how many times does your heart beat between dawn and lunchtime?
explanation: A resting heart beats about 70 times a minute, so about 4,000 times an hour.
Dawn to lunchtime is roughly six hours.
Six lots of 4,000 is 24,000, and the nearest choice on the list is 30,000.
problems.useAgain: when something steady repeats all morning and you want the total without counting any of it.
hints: How many times does a resting heart beat in one minute?
Grow one minute into one hour, then count the hours from dawn to lunch.
problems.socraticHint: Which is easier to be honest about: a whole morning of beats, or one minute of them?

variant.prompt: About how many breaths do you take between dawn and lunchtime?

problems.prompt: Suppose a C++ program does ten million loop turns in about a tenth of a second. At that speed, about how many turns would it do in one whole minute?
explanation: Ten million turns in a tenth of a second is a hundred million turns in one second.
One minute is 60 seconds.
Sixty lots of a hundred million is six thousand million, which is six billion.
problems.useAgain: when a rate is given over an awkward slice of time and you need it over a much longer one.
hints: First work out the turns in one whole second, not in a tenth of one.
Then stretch that one second up to sixty of them.
problems.socraticHint: A tenth of a second is an awkward size to think in. What size of second would make the next step easy?

variant.prompt: Suppose a Python program does ten million loop turns in about one second. About how many turns would it do in one whole minute?

problem.prompt: On the driveway you chalk a window: a big square cut into four equal panes by one line straight down the middle and one line straight across. Every line you chalked is a road, and every place two roads meet is a corner. How many corners have an odd number of roads leaving them?
explanation: Nine places on this drawing are corners: the four outside corners, the middle of each side, and the crossing point in the centre.
An outside corner has two roads leaving it, one along each side, so it is even.
The middle of a side has three: the two halves of that side, plus the line that crosses there.
The centre has four roads, one in each direction, so it is even too.
That leaves the four side middles, and nothing else is odd.
problem.useAgain: when a drawing has to be checked before you try to trace it, because counting roads at each corner is faster than trying.
hints: Walk the drawing with a finger and stop everywhere two lines meet, including the middle of each side.
Count the roads leaving each kind of corner separately: the outside ones, the side middles, then the centre.
problem.socraticHint: The middle of a side does not look like a corner. What makes it one anyway?

variant.prompt: You chalk a bigger window: a big square cut into nine equal panes by two lines down and two lines across. How many corners have an odd number of roads leaving them?

steps.title: Inequalities finished: two ends at once, and the sign that turns

problems.prompt: Solve for x with legal moves only: x - 4 >= 9. Which line says the answer?
explanation: An inequality is two pans that do not balance, and the same move on both keeps the heavier side heavier.
Add 4 to both sides. The left becomes x and the right becomes 13.
So x is 13, or anything larger than 13.
Check with 13: 13 take away 4 is 9, and 9 is 9 or more, so 13 belongs.
problems.useAgain: when an inequality has a number added to or taken from the letter and nothing else.
hints: Something has been taken away from x. What undoes taking away?
Do it to both sides, and notice that adding the same amount to both never changes which side is bigger.
problems.socraticHint: You have solved equations like this for a year. What is the one thing an inequality asks you to watch that an equation never did?

variant.prompt: Solve for y: y - 6 > 5. Which line says the answer?

problems.prompt:
Ravi solved -3x + 7 > 25 like this:
Line 1: Take 7 away from both sides: -3x > 18.
Line 2: Divide both sides by -3: x > -6.
Line 3: The smallest whole number that fits is -5, since -6 itself is not included.
Line 4: Whole numbers greater than -6 all fit the inequality: -5, -4, -3, and so on.
Which line is wrong?
explanation: Line 2 is wrong: dividing by a negative flips an inequality, so it reads x less than -6, not x greater than -6.
Lines 1, 3 and 4 are each done correctly for the range they were given. They just build correctly on the wrong range Line 2 handed them.
The true range is x less than -6, so the smallest whole number is not -5, since -5 is not less than -6.
Multiplying or dividing both sides of an inequality by a negative number flips which way the sign points, every single time.
problems.useAgain: when solving an inequality forces you to multiply or divide both sides by a negative number.
hints: Every arithmetic step here is done correctly. The trouble is in what happens to the inequality sign itself.
Dividing both sides of an inequality by a negative number is not the same move as dividing an equation by one.
problems.socraticHint: Test the boundary number itself in the very first inequality. Does it actually work, and on which side of it do the true answers sit?

variant.prompt:
Zara solved -5x - 2 > 13 like this:
Line 1: Add 2 to both sides: -5x > 15.
Line 2: Divide both sides by -5, flipping the sign: x < -3.
Line 3: Check with x = -4: -5 times -4 is 20, minus 2 is 22, and 22 is more than 13, so -4 works.
Line 4: Check with x = -2: -5 times -2 is 10, minus 2 is 8, and 8 is not more than 13, so -2 does not work.
Which line is wrong?

problems.prompt: Start with 4 < 10, which is true. Multiply both sides by -1 and put both answers on a number line. Which statement is true now?
explanation: On the number line -4 sits four steps left of zero and -10 sits ten steps left.
Further left means smaller, so -10 is the smaller one now and -4 is the larger.
Now do it with a legal move instead of a picture. Start again from 4 < 10.
Add -4 and -10 to both sides. Adding the same to both never changes which side is bigger.
The left becomes -10, the right becomes -4, so -10 < -4, which is -4 > -10.
The flip is not a new rule. It is what adding to both sides already said.
problems.useAgain: when both sides of an inequality are multiplied or divided by a negative number.
hints: Do not decide this from a rule. Put both new numbers on a number line first.
Which of the two sits further to the left, and what does further left mean about size?
problems.socraticHint: Nothing changed about the two numbers themselves. So what exactly did multiplying by a negative do to the line they sit on?

variant.prompt: Start with 2 < 6, which is true. Multiply both sides by -3. Which statement is true now?

problems.prompt: Solve -2x > 14. What is the largest integer x that makes it true? An integer is a whole number or the negative of one, so integers run to the left of zero as well as to the right.
explanation: Share both sides by -2. Dividing by a negative turns the line around, so the sign turns: x is less than -7.
Less than -7 means further left than -7, and the first integer further left is -8.
Check: -2 times -8 is 16, and 16 is more than 14.
The trap is leaving the sign alone and answering x is more than -7, which fails that check.
problems.useAgain: when the number stuck to the letter is negative and has to be divided away.
hints: The number stuck to x is negative. That matters more here than anything else.
Divide both sides by it, then ask what the sign is obliged to do.
problems.socraticHint: There are two things to get right here and only one of them is arithmetic. What is the other?

variant.prompt: Solve -3x >= 12. What is the largest integer x that makes it true?

problems.prompt: How many whole numbers x make 3 < x + 1 <= 8 true?
explanation: A compound inequality is two conditions at once, and x has to satisfy both of them.
Take 1 from all three parts: x is more than 2, and x is 7 or less.
More than 2 shuts 2 out. Seven or less lets 7 in.
So x can be 3, 4, 5, 6 or 7, which is five whole numbers.
problems.useAgain: when a letter is trapped between two bounds and the question asks how many values fit.
hints: Whatever move you make, make it to all three parts, not just to two of them.
Then write out the whole numbers the two ends allow, and count what you wrote.
problems.socraticHint: One end of this range lets its boundary in and the other shuts it out. Which is which, and how does the sign tell you?

variant.prompt: How many whole numbers x make 5 <= x + 2 < 11 true?

problems.prompt: A number line is drawn with an open circle at 2, a filled circle at 7, and the stretch between them shaded. Which inequality is that picture?
explanation: An open circle marks a boundary the answer gets close to but never reaches.
A filled circle marks a boundary that is allowed in.
Open at 2 gives x more than 2. Filled at 7 gives x at most 7.
Written together: 2 is less than x, and x is 7 or less.
problems.useAgain: when a solution arrives as a picture and has to be written down, or the other way round.
hints: Decide what each circle means on its own, before you look at the four lines offered.
One end is shut out and the other is let in. Which end is which?
problems.socraticHint: If the answer were allowed to be exactly 2, what would the picture have to look like instead?

variant.prompt: A number line has a filled circle at -3, an open circle at 4, and the stretch between them shaded. Which inequality is that picture?

problems.prompt: Suppose a table at the summer market costs 14 dollars, and every bracelet you sell brings in 3 dollars. How many bracelets do you have to sell before the money taken in is more than the table cost?
explanation: Money taken in is 3 dollars a bracelet, so n bracelets bring in 3n dollars.
That has to beat the table, so 3n is more than 14.
Share both sides by 3, which is positive, so the sign stays put: n is more than 4 and two thirds.
Bracelets come whole, so the first n that clears the table is 5, bringing in 15 dollars.
problems.useAgain: when a cost has to be caught up with and the thing you sell only comes in whole units.
hints: Write the money taken in as an expression before you write any inequality.
Solving it leaves a fraction, and you cannot sell part of a bracelet.
problems.socraticHint: The inequality hands you a number that is not whole. Which way do you have to move from it, and why is only one direction allowed?

variant.prompt: Suppose the table costs 20 dollars and every bracelet brings in 6 dollars. How many bracelets before the money taken in is more than the table cost?

steps.title: Slope as a steady per, and every pair that shakes hands once

problems.prompt: A segment runs from (1, 2) to (4, 11). What is its slope, as a fraction in lowest terms?
explanation: Slope is the change in y over the change in x, the per for this line.
Change in y is 11 minus 2, which is 9. Change in x is 4 minus 1, which is 3.
9 over 3 is 3.
problems.useAgain: when two points on a line are known and the line's slope is the missing piece.
hints: Find the change in y between the two points, then the change in x.
Divide the change in y by the change in x.
problems.socraticHint: Does it matter which point you call first, as long as you subtract both coordinates in the same order?

variant.prompt: A segment runs from (2, 5) to (6, 13). What is its slope, as a fraction in lowest terms?

problems.prompt: A segment runs from (2, 8) to (5, -1). What is its slope, as a fraction in lowest terms?
explanation: Change in y is -1 minus 8, which is -9. Change in x is 5 minus 2, which is 3.
-9 over 3 is -3.
A negative slope means the line falls as it moves right, instead of climbing.
problems.useAgain: when a line falls from left to right, giving a negative change in y and so a negative slope.
hints: Find the change in y first; notice it is a drop, not a rise.
Divide that negative change in y by the change in x.
problems.socraticHint: If a line drops as it goes right, what sign should its slope end up with?

variant.prompt: A segment runs from (1, 10) to (3, 2). What is its slope, as a fraction in lowest terms?

problems.prompt: 8 people at a party each shake hands with every other person exactly once. How many handshakes happen in total?
explanation: Every handshake is really an unordered pair of people, since Ann shaking Bo's hand is the same handshake as Bo shaking Ann's.
Counting every different pair from the 8 people gives 28 handshakes.
problems.useAgain: when every pair from a group meets exactly once, since the total is the count of unordered pairs, not ordered ones.
hints: Is Ann shaking Bo's hand a different handshake from Bo shaking Ann's?
Count every different unordered pair among the 8 people.
problems.socraticHint: Does a handshake happen twice between the same two people, once for each direction?

variant.prompt: 10 people at a party each shake hands with every other person exactly once. How many handshakes happen in total?

problems.prompt: A chess club has 9 members. How many different 2-player games can be arranged, where order does not matter?
explanation: A game between Ann and Bo is the same matchup as a game between Bo and Ann.
Counting every different unordered pair from the 9 members gives 36 possible games.
problems.useAgain: when matchups from a bigger group are counted, and switching which player is named first does not create a new matchup.
hints: Would naming the two players in the opposite order create a different game?
Count every different unordered pair from the 9 members.
problems.socraticHint: Does the board look any different depending on which player's name is said first?

variant.prompt: A chess club has 5 members. How many different 2-player games can be arranged, where order does not matter?

steps.title: The odd corner rule on real streets, and your first puzzle set for someone else

problems.prompt: Invent your own handshake-style counting puzzle: pick a number of people for a gathering, decide the rule (for example, everyone shakes hands with everyone else exactly once, or everyone trades stickers with everyone else exactly once), and work out the total yourself first. Write the puzzle down as you would hand it to someone else, state your one correct total, then prove it using the every-pair-twice idea: explain why counting from every person doubles every pair, and show the exact division that undoes that doubling.

mustMention: the number of people I chose
counting from every person doubles each pair
dividing by two undoes the doubling

explanation: Setting this puzzle means picking the group size first, then finding its total honestly, before anybody else sees the question.
Counting from every single person gives group size times one less than the group, and that counts every pair from both of its ends.
Dividing that by two undoes the double count, since each handshake was counted exactly twice, once from each side.
A puzzle with a wrong total is broken, so check your own answer with a small group you can count by hand.
problems.useAgain: when you want to build your own counting puzzle and prove its total is right before you show it to anyone.
hints: Pick your group size and your rule before you write a single word of the puzzle.
Count every handshake from both ends first, then say what has to be done to undo that doubling.
problems.socraticHint: If you handed your puzzle to a friend, could they check your total using a group so small they could just draw it?

problems.prompt: A friend says: I drew a shape, and exactly one of its corners has an odd number of roads. Is that possible?
explanation: Add up the number of roads at every corner of any drawing at all.
Every road has two ends, so it adds one at each end, and the grand total is exactly twice the number of roads.
Twice anything is even, so that grand total is always even.
A single odd count with only even counts beside it would make the total odd, so odd corners always come in pairs.
Exactly one odd corner cannot happen. No such drawing exists to be drawn.
problems.useAgain: when a claim counts something at every corner, because each connection gets counted from both of its ends.
hints: Add the road counts at every corner and ask what that grand total is really counting.
Each road gets counted at both of its ends. What does that force the total to be?
problems.socraticHint: Your friend is certain he drew it, and you have not seen it. If you tried and failed to draw one yourself, would that settle the question either way?

variant.prompt: A friend says: I drew a shape, and exactly four of its corners have an odd number of roads. Is that possible?

problems.prompt: A block like yours has five crossings where streets meet. Crossing A has 4 streets, B has 3, C has 3, D has 2 and E has 2. A postman wants to walk every street exactly once. Which is true?
options: It cannot be done, because two crossings are odd.
It can be done, but only starting at B or at C.
It can be done, and it does not matter where he starts.
It can be done, but only starting at A.
explanation: Two crossings are odd, B and C, and the other three are even.
A crossing he only passes through is entered and left, so it spends streets two at a time and has to be even.
The odd ones cannot be passed through, so they can only be the two ends of the walk.
So the walk exists, and it starts at B and finishes at C, or the other way round.
problems.useAgain: when a route has to cover every street or every line exactly once and you want to know before you set off.
hints: Sort the crossings into odd and even before you think about any route at all.
A crossing in the middle of a walk is entered and then left, so its streets get used two at a time.
problems.socraticHint: What is true of the very first crossing and the very last one that is not true of any crossing in between?

variant.prompt: A different block also has five crossings: A has 3 streets, B has 3, C has 3, D has 3 and E has 2. Can the postman walk every street exactly once?
options: No, because four crossings are odd.
Yes, but only starting at E.
Yes, but only starting at A and ending at B.

problems.prompt: A chalk drawing has exactly four corners with an odd number of roads, and all of it is joined up. You may chalk in extra roads between corners. What is the smallest number of extra roads that makes the whole thing traceable in one stroke?
explanation: An extra road changes the count at exactly the two corners it joins, and nowhere else.
Chalk it between two of the odd corners and both of them turn even.
That leaves two odd corners, which is exactly what a one stroke walk allows.
Chalking nothing is not enough, because four odd corners is more than two.
problems.useAgain: when a drawing fails the odd corner test and you are allowed to change the drawing instead of the walk.
hints: Each extra road you chalk changes the count at two corners, never at just one.
You are allowed to finish with two odd corners. So how many of them do you actually need to get rid of?
problems.socraticHint: Which corners would you join, and what does adding a road do to a corner's count?

variant.prompt: A joined up drawing has exactly eight corners with an odd number of roads. What is the smallest number of extra roads that makes it traceable in one stroke?

problems.prompt: A peak, untimed. At a family gathering everyone shook hands with everyone else exactly once, and there were 28 handshakes in all. How many people were there?
explanation: Each person shakes hands with everyone except themselves, so with one fewer than the whole group.
Counting outwards from everybody counts each handshake twice, once from each end.
So the handshake total is the group size times one less, then halved.
Halving gave 28, so the group times one less is 56, and 8 times 7 is 56.
problems.useAgain: when every pair in a group does something once and you are handed the total instead of the group size.
hints: Every handshake gets counted twice if you count outwards from each person in turn.
Double the 28 first, then hunt for two numbers next to each other that multiply to it.
problems.socraticHint: If one more person walked in, how many new handshakes would that one person add?

variant.prompt: A peak, untimed. At a club meeting everyone shook hands with everyone else exactly once, and there were 45 handshakes. How many people were there?

problems.prompt: A second peak, untimed. How many whole numbers n make 5 < 2n - 1 < 20 true?
explanation: Add 1 to all three parts: 6 is less than 2n, and 2n is less than 21.
Halve all three parts: n is more than 3, and n is less than 10 and a half.
More than 3 shuts 3 out. Less than 10 and a half lets 10 in.
So n runs from 4 up to 10, which is seven whole numbers.
problems.useAgain: when a letter is squeezed between two bounds and the count of the values matters more than the range.
hints: Peel the parts away one move at a time, and do every move to all three pieces at once.
When you land on two ends, decide separately for each whether its own boundary is allowed in.
problems.socraticHint: Once you know the two ends, is counting the whole numbers between them the same job as subtracting one from the other?

variant.prompt: A second peak, untimed. How many whole numbers n make 2 < 3n - 4 < 20 true?

problems.prompt: Start with the street map of your own block. Mark a dot everywhere streets meet, write the number of streets at each dot, and say whether a postman could walk every street on your block exactly once. Then design a one stroke puzzle of your own for the family, and prove your own answer before you show it to anyone. Draw it in the field journal. Write the road count beside every corner, say how many corners are odd, and say from that whether it can be traced and where a tracer would have to begin. Then say what you changed while you were designing it, and why.

mustMention: the road count written beside every corner, on my own street map and on my drawing
how many of those corners are odd
whether each one can be traced in one stroke, and where the start has to be
that my drawing is joined up, with nothing the pencil would have to jump to

explanation: Setting a puzzle is harder than solving one, because you have to know the answer before the drawing exists.
So start from the corners, not the picture: decide how many odd corners you want, then build a drawing that has them.
Zero or two odd corners makes a traceable puzzle. Four or more makes an impossible one, and both are fair to set.
The count only settles it if the whole drawing is one piece. Two separate loops have no odd corners at all, and the pencil would still have to jump between them.
Your proof is the corner count itself, written out corner by corner, because that is the only evidence anyone else can check.
A puzzle you cannot prove is a guess you are asking your family to share.
problems.useAgain: when you set a puzzle for somebody else and have to be certain of the answer before they start.
hints: Decide the answer first, traceable or not. The drawing comes second.
Build the corners you want, join them up, then count what you actually drew rather than what you meant to draw.
problems.socraticHint: What would make your puzzle unfair, and is unfair the same thing as hard?

steps.title: Explain it in writing: why the sign turns
steps.prompt: Write why multiplying both sides of an inequality by a negative number turns the sign around. Start with one true inequality of your own choosing and a number line drawn underneath it. Show where both sides land after the multiplying, say which one is now further left, and say why further left settles which is bigger. Then say what would go wrong if you left the sign where it was. Then do it a second way with no picture at all: take your inequality and add the opposite of each side to both sides, and show that the same swap falls out of a move you already had. Finish with the one sentence you would say to somebody who has only ever been told to flip it.

steps.title: Explain it out loud
steps.prompt: Record yourself running one person through the one stroke puzzle you designed, with the drawing in shot. Point at each corner and say its road count out loud, say how many came out odd, and say that the whole drawing is joined up with nothing the pencil would have to jump to. Then say whether it can be traced and where they would have to start. Do not tell them the rule before they have tried it themselves.
